definition: Bad-tempered and sulky in a childish way, especially over small annoyances.
example: After losing the coin toss, the captain gave a petulant shrug and refused to shake hands.
nuance: Petulant points to childish sulking over something minor, while irritable means a person is generally easy to annoy.
prompt: A teenager is told he cannot borrow the family car this weekend.
options: He gave a petulant sigh, slammed his door, and skipped dinner in protest.
He gave a petulant nod, thanked his parents warmly, and offered to take the bus.
He raised a petulant point about the bus schedule that settled the matter fairly.
He made a calm, petulant case, listing three reasons he would drive carefully.
reasons: Sighing, slamming doors, and sulking through dinner over a small letdown is childish bad temper.
Accepting the news warmly and without complaint is the reverse of sulky behavior.
This treats the word as if it meant pertinent; a relevant, fair point has nothing sulky about it.
A calm, reasoned argument has none of the pouting, childish edge the word requires.

practice.prompt: A chef reads a review saying her soup was slightly too salty.
options: The petulant chef thanked the critic politely and adjusted the seasoning the very next morning.
The petulant aroma of garlic drifted from the kitchen into the dining room.
The petulant chef quietly spent a year studying salt to master the balance.
The petulant chef pulled the soup from the menu and sulked in her office all night.
reasons: Polite thanks and a quick fix show maturity, the opposite of sulkiness.
The word describes moody people or behavior, not smells; this confuses it with pungent.
Patient, disciplined effort to improve is grown-up, not a childish fit of temper.
Overreacting to mild criticism by pouting and withdrawing shows childish ill temper.
